instruments.name: data_loader_mnist
instruments.what_it_decides: Whether the MNIST dataset loaded by data.load_mnist matches the paper's own dataset by fingerprint -- size (50k/10k/10k x 784), vocabulary (labels exactly {0..9}), pixel range ([0,1] f32), and a checksum (pixel sums) that a synthetic / all-zeros / wrong-corpus substitute cannot match. A closed-book run that fell back to a 65-token synthetic corpus passed every downstream gate and meant nothing; this fingerprint prevents that. data.check_mnist_fingerprint (called inside load_mnist) raises AssertionError on any mismatch, never returns a boolean. data.check_mnist_3v7_fingerprint verifies the 3-vs-7 subset (only {-1,+1}, +1 == digit 3).
instruments.requires_tools: network (MNIST IDX download from ossci-datasets S3 mirror)

instruments.name: data_loader_cifar10
instruments.what_it_decides: Whether CIFAR-10 loaded by data.load_cifar10 is the real dataset by fingerprint -- size (45k/5k/10k x 3072), vocabulary (labels {0..9} int64), dtype float32, per-image GCN (each image centered by its own mean, one global scale to std ~0.5; the pylearn2 GlobalContrastNormalization form the paper's footnote 2 references, tex:343-345), a per-image-mean~0 sanity, a per-pixel-variance structural check, AND a RAW uint8 pixel-sum checksum in _load_cifar_raw (a property the GCN recipe cannot force -- the CIFAR analogue of the MNIST checksum). data.check_cifar10_fingerprint (called inside load_cifar10) raises on a non-GCN / wrong-dim / wrong-label / synthetic-corpus array. The raw checksum rejects a std-matched synthetic corpus that the post-GCN structural checks alone might miss.
instruments.status_note: The 170 MB CIFAR-10 tar downloads on first use (slow link ~75 KB/s in this env); load_cifar10 unpacks it, applies PER-IMAGE GCN, and the fingerprint (per-image-mean~0 + per-pixel-variance spread + the raw uint8 checksum in _load_cifar_raw) passes. The positive test test_cifar10_real runs (not skipped) when the tar is present and the cifar_conv_maxout arm runs on the real data -- no synthetic substitution. The negative test (rejects synthetic / non-GCN / wrong-dim) runs without the download.

instruments.name: selfcheck_claims
instruments.what_it_decides: For each claim in claims.json, whether the measured value (or sequence, for curve claims) satisfies the claim's assertion (value/ordering/existence/invariant/curve) at every seed. Renders pass/fail/blocked and writes selfcheck.json with a produced_by=selfcheck_claims.py stamp. A blocked or failed HIGH claim makes the gate exit non-zero; a grader that cannot run (malformed measured.json) raises a traceback rather than emitting a verdict. This is the reproduction's OWN self-check grader and writes selfcheck.json -- never claims_result.json, which the workflow's numbers gate owns (a script here writing that filename would collide with the gate and be refused).
instruments.requires_tools: none (pure python; reads claims.json + measured.json). The gate is exercised through sys.executable in an isolated temp dir (tests/test_selfcheck_claims.py), never by shelling out to bare `python` -- the 'python vs python3' mis-grading failure mode does not apply here. The negative_test is the canonical known-wrong case (verdict 'fail'); the additional_tests cover the two other negative paths the contract names -- a blocked metric is never a silent 'pass' and a grader that cannot run raises a traceback rather than a verdict.

instruments.name: logreg_analytic_equivalence
instruments.what_it_decides: c07: that FGSM is exact for logistic regression -- the CORRECT worst-case closed form zeta(eps*||w||_1 - y*(w.x+b)) equals the actual adversarial loss under the REAL gradient-based per-example FGSM attack.fgsm (sign(grad_x J) = -y*sign(w), so x_adv_i = x_i - eps*y_i*sign(w)). The paper's tex:411 form zeta(y*(eps*||w||_1 - w.x - b)) has a sign slip for y=-1 (it decreases the loss instead of maximizing it); c07 checks the CORRECTED form, not the paper's. The positive test asserts |real-FGSM loss - corrected analytic form| < 1e-4 on a fixed batch with MIXED labels; the negative tests assert (a) a wrong-sign (+y*sign(w)) attack does NOT match, and (b) the paper's OWN tex:411 form does NOT match on mixed labels -- proving the check is not a rubber stamp and would reject the paper's slipped closed form.

instruments.name: fgsm_inf_norm
instruments.what_it_decides: That the FGSM perturbation satisfies ||eta||_inf == eps exactly (tex:309) with sign(0):=0 and NO clipping of x_adv (SPEC sec 4.9: x_adv may exceed [0,1]). The positive tests assert max|eta| == eps, every perturbed pixel is exactly eps, and x_adv is not clipped; the negative test asserts a clipping implementation and a scaled (0.5*eps) perturbation are both rejected by those assertions.

instruments.name: degeneracy_check
instruments.what_it_decides: That the method at its no-op setting reproduces the baseline EXACTLY (bit-identical weights via torch.equal): adversarial eps=0, noise eps=0, and L1 coef=0 each reduce to plain training. The cheapest real correctness evidence -- catches a mis-wired adversarial/noise/L1 loop in seconds. The negative test asserts that with eps>0 (a genuinely non-degenerate run) the weights DIFFER from baseline, so the check is sensitive to a leak rather than a rubber stamp.

instruments.name: rubbish_any_prob_threshold
instruments.what_it_decides: Whether a model assigns any class probability > 0.5 to Gaussian rubbish inputs (tex:905-911). For softmax-top: max_k p_k > 0.5; for sigmoid-top / RBF (rows need not sum to 1): any p_k > 0.5 (equivalently max_k p_k > 0.5). The 0.5 threshold is load-bearing: a softmax scores ~100% rubbish error (the paper's result) while an RBF far from data scores ~0% -- the RBF-zero assertion is the oracle that proves the threshold is correct. The negative test shows a buggy threshold (>0.0, always true for exp-quadratic RBF) would mis-report the robust RBF as ~100% error, which the correct eval rejects.

instruments.name: retrain_from_scratch
instruments.what_it_decides: Protocol invariant (paper tex:505-506): the Phase-2 retrain-on-full-60k must restart from the INITIAL weights with a FRESH optimizer (no carried momentum), not continue from the Phase-1 state. The positive test asserts the Phase-2 starting state is BIT-IDENTICAL to the captured init state (directly detects the old continuation bug where Phase 2 resumed from the Phase-1 best_state) AND that Phase 2 actually moves off the init weights and differs from a Phase-1-only run. The negative test shows the Phase-1 best_state differs from the init (so a continuation Phase 2 would fail the phase2_start==init check), proving the guard has discriminating power.

instruments.name: adv_train_fgsm_mode
instruments.what_it_decides: That the in-training FGSM perturbation is computed with the model in EVAL mode (dropout OFF), per the paper's definition of FGSM on the deterministic network (tex:309, Fig.1). The positive test asserts the perturbation is non-zero on most pixels (eval mode) and that the eval-mode fraction is >50pp higher than a train-mode FGSM (which zeroes the input gradient on ~99% of pixels under p=0.99 dropout). Guards the review finding that the adversarial-training attack ran through an active dropout mask, weakening the perturbation. No separate negative_test: the contrast (eval >> train) IS the rejection of the train-mode bug.

instruments.name: model_arch_faithfulness
instruments.what_it_decides: That the model classes match the paper's equations (not an output grader, but a construction invariant that decides whether the implemented model IS the one the paper describes). RBF (tex:595): no per-class temperature and no loss clamp -- logits <= 0 => NLL >= 0 by construction, so a clamp is dead; an earlier inert log_temp slot is removed (test_rbf_has_no_log_temp_and_no_loss_clamp). Conv maxout: maxout is itself the nonlinearity, so NO ReLU is applied after a conv-maxout stage (an earlier F.relu was an extra nonlinearity the paper never describes; test_conv_maxout_has_no_post_relu).
